AML3031.title: American Literature Ⅰ
description: AML 3031 is a literary history course, focusing on broader literary movements in indigenous and British colonial America and what is now the U.S. Literature from this period uses genres and language that are less familiar to modern readers. Early American readers and publishers were suspicious of fiction and wanted “truth and beauty” instead (moral lessons and poetic forms). Poetry was an esteemed formal genre. Sermon, history, poetry, polemic, travel narrative, personal narrative, and origin story proliferated during this time.
This course covers three literary historical periods:
1) indigenous, early settlement and colonial literature;
2) the Enlightenment or “Age of Reason”; and
3) the 19th-century American “Renaissance” and “Age of Reform.”

The course addresses how specific literary texts produced during these historical periods confront questions which constitute and underpin American culture and history. Thematic focus uses origin stories.
Assignments: Weekly readings and quizzes; bi-weekly essay postings; revision of one bi-weekly essay, final exam.

AML3041.title: American Literature Ⅱ
description: POST-1865.

This semester-long webcourse surveys American Literature from the end of the Civil War to the present. It explores key literary movements such as regionalism, realism, modernism, and postmodernism, considering the ways in which each author responds to and reflects the changing world around them. We will consider the texts in their eras and in conjunction with major themes, ultimately asking what is “American Literature?”

AML3076.title: Topics in American Literature
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.
"Political Literature in the 19th Century".

This semester-long webcourse examines political literature in the long nineteenth century, beginning with antebellum abolitionist texts and ending with representations of urban conditions at the beginning of the 20th century. Students will investigate how each text responds to their contemporary political landscape, socio- and geopolitical upheavals, and a shifting understanding of the role of the Federal government. Finally, students will consider how and why these texts continue to be relevant today.

AML3261.title: Literature of the South
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This course will examine literatures written about the American South from the Antebellum period through modern-day. We will consider authors such as Kate Chopin, Zora Neale Hurston, William Faulkner, and Flannery O’Connor, among others. We will consider key movements in Southern literature and the ways in which each author defines “Southerness” and the American South’s storied but haunted history.

AML3286.title: Early American Women's Words
description: PRE-1865 and DIVERSITY.

Until the 1980s, anthologies of American literature included only Bradstreet and Emily Dickinson as American women authors before 1900. However, many colonial American women wrote and were published, sometimes in genres that are less familiar to us now.

We will study poems, letters, petitions, epitaphs, speeches, sampler verses, broadsides, journals, diaries, commonplace books, household manuals, travelogues, captivity narratives, and more by early modern women living in colonial America and the newly formed U.S.
Required tasks: Heavy reading, weekly quizzes, midterm, final project, bi-weekly essays, one of which will be revised into a formal essay for a grade.

AML3614.title: Topics in African American Lit
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

The goal of this course is to attempt to answer certain questions raised by the African-American presence in American life through its literature. By addressing issues of identity and ethnicity; in other words, looking at the implications of what it means to be “African American” as explored through literature, we will try to unravel and situate the larger construct within literary modernity, of the relationship between race and art in a meaningful way. In other words, this course will raise such important questions as, how does the African-American or Black artist negotiate what Du Bois once theorized and concluded to be the “strangeness of being black in America?” What is “the Blackness of Blackness?” and of course, how does African-American literature negotiate that complicated but foundational thesis of the Du Boisian, “double consciousness,” in its relationship with a general American reality, a well indeed as the Black Atlantic? At the end of this semester we may come to some understanding of the aesthetic as well as historical, and even political dimensions of African-American literature by examining how African American writers have used different artistic and narrative techniques to raise questions, explore, and even expand the relationship between history and art.

AML3632.title: Puerto Rican Literature
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This class will survey literature by Puerto Rican writers both on the island and on the mainland starting with authors seeking freedom from Spanish Colonial rule followed by those writing against American political and cultural domination, to the “Bootstraps” generation, through the Nuyorican poets, and up to contemporary spoken word artists. This class seeks to provide a general interdisciplinary survey of Puerto Rican cultural production including a variety of genre such as poetry, fiction, non-fiction (including speeches and newspaper columns), drama, and film. Using a chronological procedure and contextual process, we will explore the socio-political and economic factors leading to Puerto Rican migration to the mainland with a particular focus on Puerto Ricans in Central Florida.

AML3640.title: Native American Literature
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

In contrast to the often romantic depiction of the American Indian in history or films, this course surveys Native American literature from its traditional origins—including tales, songs, and oratory—to more modern responses in autobiography, fiction, poetry, and other contemporary genres by writers such as N. Scott Momaday and Louise Erdrich. In addition to learning about an alternate, indigenous history and culture of North America and the “oral tradition” in different periods and regions, this course aims to explore a series of thematic and aesthetic continuities and to understand the various issues that Native Americans face both on and off reservation communities today. This course uses You Tube and other media as part of its instruction. Course requirements include reading, discussion posts, brief written responses, a course paper, and a final exam.

(Note: This course fulfills post-1865 “Literary History” and diversity requirements. To enroll in this course you must have previously taken ENC1101 and ENC 1102. ENG 3014 is highly recommended, but not required.)

AML3643.title: Cont Native Amer Prose & Poetr
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This upper-level literary history course covers contemporary Native American literature since 1970. Our historical focus starts with the so-called “second wave” of Native American nonfiction, novels, poetry, and short fiction.

We will read six books by Native American authors and consider how these works express a range of perspectives on contemporary Native American presence and history; relationship to land; and representations and cultural survivance. Required tasks: Two short papers; midterm; final; bi-weekly discussion postings.

AML4300.title: Major American Authors
description: POST-1865 (or MAJOR AUTHOR) and DIVERSITY.
Catalog: “A comprehensive study of selected major American literary figures.”

AML 4300 (RI) is an asynchronous online course focused on the works of acclaimed contemporary Chickasaw writer and ecofeminist Linda Hogan. We will read Hogan’s poetry, essays, memoir, and three of her novels.

This course has a Research Intensive designation that will appear on your UCF transcript. This designation is one of UCF’s four High Impact practices and challenges students to engage actively in research processes underlying professional work in the discipline of literary studies. 30% of the final grade is based on the final research paper you will submit; 20% of the course grade is based on the successful completion of stepped research assignments; 5% of the course grade is based on a final poster presentation about your research project. Each step of this research process will be completed in scaffolded assignments that require students to produce documents used in literary research. Three 750-word essays; weekly quizzes; one conference length (10-12 page; 2500-word) essay with research; heavy reading load.

CRW3010H.title: Honors Creative Writing
description: Only open to Honors College students. Applies toward English major or minor as required class (equivalent to CRW 3013).In this honors-level introductory course students will practice writing, reading, and responding to works of poetry, fiction, and creative nonfiction. Organized in three five-week units, students will begin working with the smallest possible unit of output in the given genre (six-word stories, for instance, in fiction) and ending reading a book-length work. Students will submit works of poetry, fiction, and creative nonfiction for both small-group peer review and full-class discussion. By the end of the course, students will have learned and applied critical vocabulary in all three genres, written responses to their own and their peers' work, and prepared themselves for genre-specific creative-writing courses.

CRW3013.title: Creative Writing for English M
description: This class is designed to introduce foundational elements of craft through critical reading, thoughtful critique and discussion of peer writing, and practice. Together, we will explore several essential creative concepts across three units: fiction, poetry, and creative nonfiction.

CRW3053.title: Thry & Practice Creative Wrtng
description: In this entry-level course, students will read literary texts to feed their understanding of authorial decisions in contemporary writing in fiction, literary nonfiction, scriptwriting, and poetry. Students will become fluent in relevant writing terminology and concepts, gain insight into the emphases and specialties of the UCF creative writing program, identify possible career paths and “uses” of a degree in English with a specialization in creative writing; and familiarize themselves with the publishing process.

CRW3120.title: Fiction Writing Workshop Ⅰ
description: This course focuses on short fiction. We’ll read, analyze, and discuss published stories, as well as workshop original stories of our own. Students will prepare written feedback (workshop notes) for story submissions and engage in rigorous group discussion. Over the course of the semester, students will write and submit two original short stories of approximately 2500 words each.

Learning goals include gaining familiarity with contemporary fiction, learning techniques to write successful original fiction, and learning how to constructively analyze and revise drafts of original fiction in terms of character and storyline, while considering foundational elements of craft such as effective characterization, point of view, dialogue, and plot.

As one would expect with a workshop, the course will involve a lot of group discussion, in which everyone is expected to participate. Solid participation will require the stories, both published and student-submitted, be read and considered deeply prior to the class period in which they are up for discussion. In this way, we can all learn together, with the outcome being we improve our own stories as well as our editorial acumen.

CRW3211.title: Creative Nonfiction Workshop Ⅰ
description: This course is for students interested in turning lived experience into compelling writing. We’ll read contemporary essays and experiment with scene, voice, image, reflection, structure, and research, then try those techniques in two longer essays. The class includes frequent writing exercises, peer workshop, and a final portfolio of revised creative nonfiction.

CRW3310.title: Poetry Writing Workshop Ⅰ
description: This course is for students who want to read, write, and experiment with contemporary poetry. We’ll study how poets use image, sound, line, form, voice, and other elements of craft, then try those techniques in our own work. The class is highly generative and includes writing exercises, peer workshop, and a final portfolio of revised original poems. No particular style—or prior identity as a “poet”—is required.

CRW3311.title: Readings in Poetry for Crw
description: This course is an Online course. This means that we shall have our class conducted online. We will read from a variety of poetry from across the world, that reflects the plurality of the poetic experience and its many traditions. We shall read these poems closely, examine their formal structure, and identify textual variety in poetry. The course is not designed as a historical survey but as a general, exploratory discussion on the art and craft of poetry. Its approach is to engage and examine poetry from various directions – as a shapely product of the imagination; as a form of distinct utterance - public and private, as highly stylized and aesthetically arranged exploration into unique psychological worlds, and as a product of a social moment. Generally, poetry offers intellectual stimulation, linguistic pleasures, as well as moral insights. It presents, as well, its own unique aesthetic and interpretive difficulties, perhaps because it radiates between two zones of reality - our private lives as readers, and our public lives as writers. Students will engage in extensive discussions about the making of poems as well as understand the elements that make poetic production possible: that is the aesthetic, social, cultural, historical and political conditions to which the poetic imagination responds. We will analyze poetry from the 20th-century poetry to now. The course attempts to take into broad account the traditional elements of poetry and their contemporary alternatives. There will be weekly writing assignments, including some exercises in poetic craft.

CRW3610.title: Scriptwriting Workshop Ⅰ
description: Theory and practice of writing short scripts for film.

This course thoroughly introduces studying, learning, and practicing screenwriting techniques. We will learn about screenplay structure, analyze dramatic strategies in film, learn and apply correct script form, and creatively engage in the various stages of original scriptwriting.
THIS IS NOT A COURSE TO DEVELOP A FEATURE FILM SCRIPT OR A TELEVISION PILOT.

CRW3713.title: Writing for Video Games
description: This Integrative-Learning Experience (IE) course will introduce students to the basic theories and practices associated with game design, including brainstorming, the elements of gameplay, artificial intelligence, and storytelling within dynamic, interactive systems. Articles written by experts in the field will be analyzed as we explore the challenges and pitfalls of attempting to merge narratives with games. Students will conceive and outline their own game and produce interactive scripts for elements such as cut scenes and scripted events to be workshopped in class. Each student will produce a 30–40-page Game Design Document (GDD) for an original game with an emphasis on narrative design (since this is a writing course). Student learning outcomes include being able to analyze theories of game design and recognize how they influence narratives within games; justify effective writing techniques for developing original video games; solve design issues such as creating player agency and addressing linearity in story development; manage the design phase of a game by creating a goal-based writing schedule to achieve each milestone; refine and adapt game pitches for peers, the instructor, and industry professionals beyond UCF; compile game design documents that demonstrates mastery of course content; and reflect on design work and how it might be used in game development communities around the globe.

CRW3950.title: Cypress Dome Editorship
description: Participating within The Cypress Dome requires at least two in-person semesters (fall 2026 and spring 2027) at UCF. Only students in the current fall 2026 class can enroll in the spring 2027 semester.

CRW4122.title: Fiction Writing Workshop Ⅱ
description: This course focuses on short fiction.

We’ll read, analyze, and discuss published stories, as well as workshop original stories of our own. Students will prepare written feedback (workshop notes) for story submissions and engage in rigorous group discussion. Over the course of the semester, students will write and submit two original short stories of approximately 3500 words each.

Learning goals include gaining familiarity with contemporary fiction, learning techniques to write successful original fiction, and learning how to constructively analyze and revise drafts of original fiction in terms of character, structure, and language, while considering foundational elements of literary craft such as effective characterization, story shape, point of view, dialogue, and sentence-level language choices.

As one would expect with a workshop, the course will involve a lot of group discussion, in which everyone is expected to participate. Solid participation will require the stories, both published and student-submitted, be read and considered deeply prior to the class period in which they are up for discussion. In this way, we can all learn together, with the outcome being we improve our own stories as well as our editorial acumen.

CRW4125.title: Worldbuilding
description: What makes a world? What strategies can we use as writers to craft worlds that are immersive, “lived-in,” and compelling? In this course, we’ll ask a lot of questions about our world as well as the worlds we build on the page. We’ll read a mixture of fiction, essays, theory, and poetry. This course will likely include a trip to the university archives. You can expect a lot of in-class writing and sharing; this is a generative class and may include a workshop unit. Over the course of the semester, we will build a world as a class and write a full-length project in it. A large amount of collaboration and collaborative writing is required for this course. Anyone who takes this course should be prepared to regularly contribute to our collaborative world-building project. Your final project will be either a portfolio of original creative work or instructor-approved self-designed project.

CRW4224.title: Creative Nonfict Workshop Ⅱ
description: This is a workshop-based course in literary nonfiction (memoir, personal essay, and—in some semesters—literary journalism). We’ll focus on craft-based discussions of new student writing and studies of selected published works as a way of informing our understanding of craft. Students will write sketches, full manuscripts, and craft studies. Reading is expected to include: The Boys of My Youth, by Jo Ann Beard; The Best American Essays 2013, edited by Cheryl Strayed; A Self Made of Words, by Carl Klaus, and selected online journals of nonfiction.

CRW4320.title: Poetry Writing Workshop Ⅱ
description: In this course, students will gain a deeper understanding of contemporary poetry by analyzing full-length poetry collections and participating in workshop. Building on concepts from CRW 3310, this course will challenge students within the bounds of poetry, placing equal emphasis on generative writing and close reading of texts through writing exercises, reading annotations, workshop drafts, workshop feedback, and student-led discussions. The semester will culminate in two major assignments: an "In Tandem" collaborative poetry chapbook project, written throughout the semester outside of class, and a final portfolio, which includes revised poems from workshop, an artist statement, and a publication plan.

CRW4616.title: Scriptwriting Workshop Ⅱ
description: This is an advanced-level scriptwriting workshop for English majors. It includes intensive writing practice in screenwriting, peer critique group discussion of original manuscripts, and research on the screenwriting industry. We will also view films and read the scripts of films to get a deeper understanding of formatting and story structure. In this course, we will discuss how to write scripts well and examine advanced scriptwriting techniques. We will also learn to read, analyze, and critique our own work and the work of our peers.

CRW4724.title: The Florida Review
description: This course allows students to function as interns for UCF’s prestigious literary journal, The Florida Review. Here, students learn by doing, focusing on editorial decisions, proofreading, organization, and journal production. This course is designed to help you as a writer (by demonstrating which stories, poems, and essays are accepted or rejected by a magazine, and why) and as an editor (by encouraging you to expand your tastes and sense of style to meet the multifaceted needs of a national magazine). Throughout the course, you will study and evaluate real submissions from working writers, and you will help those writers share their work with the world.

CRW6921.title: Multi-genre Workshop
description: In this course, we’ll read poets and essayists with highly varied backgrounds and vastly different approaches to structure, style, and content. This workshop will focus on writing as a process. Thus, you can expect a wide variety of exercises and assignments that center creativity as a skill and, occasionally, for such items as craft choices, processes, and/or writing notes to be workshopped alongside drafts. At the end of the semester, you will submit a portfolio or instructor-approved final project of your own design.

ENC3241.title: Writing for Technical Prof
description: Students will take on the role of professional technical communicators as they explore the purpose, audience, and genre conventions of technical documents across disciplines. Students will learn about the use of style, content organization, standard document formats, rhetoric, and ethics when preparing technical communications. Assignments may include writing effective correspondence, formal and informal reports, job application materials, and proposals.

ENC3241H.title: Honors Wr for Technical Prof
description: This course helps prepare you, a student in a technical profession or professional field, for the types of research, writing, and information presentation that you will encounter in your career after graduation. Writing has many purposes and uses beyond just relaying information, and even in the most concrete of professions, the facts do not “speak for themselves.” Your task as a writer is to articulate, explain, and interpret the information you are dealing with. Throughout your career, you will need to understand the social context of your writing and its audiences, and you will need to master the techniques of crafting your writing to suit your purposes and the interests of your audience. This course covers important professional writing genres, including resumes, proposals, presentations, and research reports.

This section of ENC 3241H is a designated HIP-Research-Intensive (RI) course. This designation will be noted on students’ transcripts. Research-Intensive is one of UCF’s four HIP course designations, along with Service-Learning, Integrative Learning and Global Learning. HIP courses are among the most challenging and rewarding at UCF.

ENC3258H.title: Hon Video Game Theory & Design
description: ONLY OPEN TO HONORS STUDENTS.

This course will introduce students to theoretical and applied concepts in video game design and explore the literary impact of video games on our culture. Students will critically evaluate video games as rhetorical devices and will learn techniques for dealing with particular game design strategies such as artificial intelligence, storytelling, cueing, and establishing/maintaining immersion. In order to better understand game literacies, students will be expected to produce a group-produced game design document (GDD). Using milestone presentations and game design pitches, students will be expected to contribute to multimedia presentations that outline the progress on the GDD (analogous to exec reviews / green light meetings in industry). Each contribution should emphasize the work that the student has completed to ensure he or she receives credit. More detailed description of the specific task requirements will be given in class.

ENC4215.title: Document Design and Publicatn
description: Technical Publication and Project Management focuses on the theory and practice of technical document design, including style, format, and layout. Students should expect to:

Identify and critique basic principles of page design, layout, typography, and graphics; Apply various design principles according to the document type and rhetorical situation; Schedule and plan collaborative design projects according to the best practices of project management using current project management tools; Recognize the different considerations for print and digital design; Understand and utilize company branding and style to create documents with the appropriate tone.

ENC4219.title: Tech Comm & Plain Language
description: This course focuses on how many of the strategies used for effective plain language are often the same strategies used for effective technical communication. Although plain language is not the best strategy for every communication challenge, it can be the best approach for many of them. In this course, we will investigate numerous case studies that demonstrate how audiences often benefit from plain language in technical, legal, financial, and government documents. Major assignments may include quizzes, discussions, mini case studies, a video project, and/or a plain language redesign project. To succeed in this course, students need access to the Microsoft Office Suite and Zoom (available for free to UCF students - https://it.ucf.edu/ucf-apps/), as well as a device that runs Zoom audio and video. Please check UCF Libraries and your local library for copies of the assigned texts before purchasing them.

ENC4262.title: Int Technical Communication
description: International Technical Communication focuses on the development of documentation for international audiences. Students will learn to address the challenges of communicating across cultures; they will learn to prepare documentation for translation and to create visuals for global audiences.
Upon completion of the course students will have gained valuable skills, experience, and knowledge. The course objectives are:

To develop an understanding of the challenges of international technical communication and learn key strategies to address those challenges To learn theories of intercultural communication and to understand their application in the workplace To learn to write for international audiences To learn to create visuals for international audiences To design and produce a documentation project To learn to prepare documentation for translation To develop project management skills To meet the challenges of working as part of a virtual team

ENC4265.title: Writing for Computer Industry
description: Students will learn to create different kinds of documentation for the computer industry, including programming, software development, and information technology. This course will focus on preparing students to write clear, effective messages that will allow them to succeed in a professional environment.

ENC4280.title: Technical Writing Style
description: The course covers strategies for understanding and improving writing styles, particularly for a variety of technical writing genres, including reports, proposals, web text, job documents, and procedural documentation. Students will understand and apply editing techniques at both copy- and comprehensive- levels in both weekly exercises and longer editing projects. Contemporary writing and editing technologies will also be discussed and applied.

ENC4293.title: Doc and Project Management
description: Development of a book-length project from idea to final published product. Examples may include style manuals, policies and procedures, and training manuals.

ENC4294.title: Client-based Project Managemen
description: Development of a substantial writing, editing, or revision project involving a real-world, real-client project. Students will collaborate with a client to produce a final published product. Examples may include manuals, policies and procedures, design documents for software products and other types of substantial documents.

ENC4414.title: Writing and Hypertext
description: Writing and HTML/CSS coding for online environments, hypertext architectures, and electronic literacy theory to develop a more critical and applied understanding of hypertext.

This course is a restricted elective in the Technical Communication major and Digital Humanities minor and was designed with humanities students in mind, so if you haven’t had any prior experience with hypertext technology, this is fine. All majors are welcome.

In this course, we will work on our writing skills, our Web site architecture skills, and our technical coding skills based on CSS and HTML to produce 1) a personal Web site, and 2) an informational Web site that you build from a ten-page term paper you write for this course on anything to do with digital humanities or technical communication. By the end of the semester, you will be a competent Web site technician and writer and have a strong theoretical and applied sense of how traditional texts or bodies of writing can be converted into hypertext documents that you build from scratch.

ENC4415.title: Dig Rhetorics & Mod Dialectic
description: Digital Rhetoric and the Modern Dialectic takes a humanities-based approach, exploring how rhetoric, dialectic, critical theory, art, media, and digital practices shape our understanding of technology, society, and ourselves. Rather than simply studying existing digital rhetoric, students will invent new rhetorical and dialectical practices for digital media, with a major focus on creating a “widesite”—a personalized digital tool for addressing the most pressing problems of our age. Drawing on Gregory Ulmer’s concept of “electracy,” the course examines modernist and postmodernist approaches across literature, visual art, film, music, and essays while encouraging students to experiment with style and develop new forms of writing and communication.

ENC4936.title: Topics in Tech Communication
description: Title: Qualitative User Research for Real-World Impact.

Course Description: Teaches students how to conduct rigorous qualitative research (such as interviews, focus groups, and observational research) to inform the design of impactful information products, such as public safety trackers, cybersecurity guides, or mobile apps.
Learning Objectives: Collect and code qualitative data and synthesize research findings into actionable design reports and strategic recommendations.

ENC6217.title: Technical Editing
description: In this course, we will examine the broad field of technical editing and explore how it has changed over time. After developing foundational knowledge about the history and practice of technical editing, we will spend the remainder of the semester learning about editing strategies and the function of technical editing in a range of professions. Students will have opportunities to practice technical editing individually and collaboratively. Major projects will include a special topics presentation, individual copy-editing challenges, and a final team-based substantive technical editing project. Although there are no scheduled class meetings, students in this course are expected to attend a one-on-one conference with the professor as well as 2 Zoom meetings with their team for the final editing project. By the end of the course, you should have multiple samples of your professional editing work to share with potential employers, in a portfolio, or on a professional website.

ENC6931.title: Topics in Tech Comm
description: This course investigates how key concepts such as disability, access, universal design, plain language, and ethics inform the practice of technical communication. Students consider how policy and technology changes have shaped disabled people's experiences with technical communication. Assignments prioritize audience awareness and offer opportunities to apply theory to practice. In the first eight weeks of the semester, students may be assigned 75-100 pages of reading per week. Major assignments may include individual and collaborative primary research projects, technology experiments, and live or recorded presentations. Some assignments may require the use of genAI. To succeed in this course, you need access to the MS Office Suite, MS Teams, and Zoom (available for free to UCF students - https://it.ucf.edu/ucf-apps/), as well as a device that allows you to run and record audio and video. Please check UCF Libraries and your local library for copies of the assigned texts before purchasing them.

ENC6951.title: Tech Comm Capstone
description: This capstone course will support you in creating a digital portfolio, with the overarching goal to produce and articulate a professional identity based in reflective, collaborative practices bolstered by rigorous theoretical framing. Your portfolio will contain a set of artifacts (documents you have produced) for specific audiences and purposes in alignment with your professional identity and the M.A. program in Technical Communication.

Your sense of professional identity as a competent technical communicator will vary depending on your goals and career trajectory. The capstone experience can help you to synthesize content from your work throughout the program as you recognize habits of mind, skills, and key theoretical or methodological approaches that have emerged across your programmatic experiences.

Ultimately, a well-composed portfolio demonstrates a clear sense of professional identity, ability to reflect upon and illustrate skills, and preparedness to transition to another setting (e.g., the workplace, the academy, a doctoral program).
Questions you’re invited to explore include:
• How do I develop a portfolio that showcases my rhetorical finesse, design savvy, and academic acumen?
• Why is theoretical framing important for portfolio development and artifact revision?
• How do I showcase ethical communication competencies and why does it matter in a portfolio?
• What are distinctions between an industry-, teaching-, or research-focused portfolio, and what role does academic framing play across these genre variations?

ENG3014.title: Theories and Tech of Lit Study
description: Theories of Literature is a gateway course designed to introduce students to the theory and practice of contemporary approaches to the academic study of literary and cultural texts. The course introduces you to the practice and theory of literary criticism. It covers multiple techniques of analysis, theories of interpretation, and application of critical approaches to selected works. You will learn how to apply these critical theories—drawn from a wide range of literary theorists, philosophers, cultural critics, commentators, and scholars of literature, history, and language—to a variety of different texts.

ENG3612.title: Trendslitcultural Text Studies
description: POST-1865.

This course will survey contemporary literature, examining the cross-section of literary study and media literacy in a media environment increasingly influenced by artificial intelligence. Students will consider how the skills developed through literary study are applicable across varied forms of media and genre.

ENG3831.title: Intro to Editorial Professions
description: This course is designed to provide an overview of different editorial professions. Students will learn the difference between general editing and proofreading, editing for scholarly journals, editing fiction, and editing nonfiction, such as website ‘copy’ (this means text) and copy in other digital formats. They will gain an understanding of the different roles of editors and copyeditors, as well as the difference between copyediting and proofreading. They will also learn how to work with a variety of different style guides and learn the basics of grammar and mechanics for copyediting. My follow-up course, ENG4832, offers you more hands-on experience in applying the introductory knowledge and skills you learn here.

ENG3861.title: Dig Humanities Approaches Ai
description: Fundamentals of digital humanities approaches to artificial intelligence. Students will explore the history of these technologies and their impact on culture and creativity. The course includes practical exercises to help students grasp the real-world uses and limitations of these tools in literary, cultural, and textual contexts. Students will gain insight into both the opportunities and challenges of AI for literary, cultural, and creative applications. They will learn to use AI tools in digital humanities projects to generate texts for analysis, document their own use of AI in textual, visual, and procedural work, and critically evaluate their methods. The course also encourages scholarly discussion of texts and concepts, enhancing students' interpretation, writing, and argumentation skills.

ENG4832.title: Scholarly Editing & Publishing
description: "A political view of textual scholarship locates editorial practice and theory within the broadest conceptions of literary and cultural study." Michelle R. Warren, The Politics of Textual Scholarship.

ENG 4832 teaches the skills that careers in publishing actually require, proofreading, copyediting, style-guide fluency (Chicago, MLA, APA), scholarly-journal production, and digital editing, and it treats those skills as something more than mechanical. The course's guiding idea is that editing is never neutral. Every editorial decision, from choosing a copy-text to enforcing a house style to selecting a publishing platform, is an exercise of power over meaning. It decides whose voice counts as "correct," what enters the archive, and what a text is allowed to say. You will graduate with a portfolio of genuine, marketable editorial skills and the critical self-awareness that separates an editor from a spell-checker. Across the semester we follow the field's central argument, between the intentionalist tradition (the editor recovers the author's intention) and the social-text tradition (the text is a collaborative, material object made by many hands). This course is a core requirement for the UCF Editing and Publishing Undergraduate Certificate.

ENG5009.title: Methods Bibleo & Research
description: Beyond the general aim of introducing you to a range of research methods and related professional issues in the field of English, this course has several goals.

First, it aims to review current approaches to literary and textual studies and ways, for example, that cultural studies enable us to engage texts from provocative points of view. Second, we will focus on basic tools of literary scholarship and the kinds of questions—and answers—that lead to productive library research. Our purpose in doing that is to go beyond “Google” and to become adept with the use of various print and electronic resources as well as appropriate research strategies and methods of technical communication. Third, in addition to examining specific bibliographical and textual problems, students will complete an annotated bibliography on a topic of interest; this will provide further practical experience in collecting research materials, assessing sources, and sharing scholarship. The course concludes with a collaborative digital humanities assignment using textual encoding and an examination of career paths.
Course requirements include weekly discussion postings, research and writing assignments, an annotated bibliography, and a final exam.

ENG6078.title: Contemp Movements Lct Theory
description: This course, a requirement for the Master’s degree in Literary, Cultural, and Textual Studies, will provide students with a rigorous overview of the theory and practice of contemporary approaches to the academic study of literary and cultural texts. The graduate seminar will examine many of the most prominent and influential “schools of thought” or critical theories of literature, including New Criticism, structuralism, poststucturalism/deconstruction, psychoanalysis, feminism, sexuality/queer studies, Marxism, new historicism, postcolonial theory, race and ethnic studies, reader response, disability studies, and eco-criticism. We will study explanatory texts about the various theories, along with representative texts of those theoretical approaches that have contributed to the intellectual history of English as a discipline. The seminar will act as a forum to engage with the current scholarly debate in literary and cultural studies, preparing students to work toward the construction of an advanced analytical paper in keeping with graduate-level coursework.

ENL2012.title: English Literature Ⅰ
description: This course offers a broad survey of authors, texts, and genres from the medieval period through the late eighteenth century, covering approximately 1000 years of English literature. As a survey, this class presents particular challenges, as we seek to cover a breadth of material without sacrificing depth of understanding. A wide base of knowledge, effective communication skills, and critical thinking are integral to success in virtually every discipline, both in college and beyond, and practicing these vitally important skills lays the groundwork for success in your future as you read and ponder the works of the earliest and greatest writers in the English language. To this end, it is essential that you read the assigned texts carefully.

ENL2022.title: English Literature Ⅱ
description: POST-1865.

This in-person class will cover literature written in England between 1798 and 1914. We will read poetry, drama and fiction by a diverse selection of English writers, reading the texts with a historical approach. We will consider the Romantic movement in poetry; the Victorian age; and The Age of Decadence. Writers include Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats, Tennyson, Christina Rossetti, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Shaw, Wilde and Forster.

ENL3222.title: Renaissance Women in Lit
description: PRE-1865 and DIVERSITY.

"Did Women Have a Renaissance?" (J. Kelly-Gadol). Renaissance women were often stereotypically portrayed—or objectified—as silent, chaste, pious, and obedient. Faced with many challenges, if not outright barriers, they struggled in their pursuit of knowledge and basic artistic literacy. This course, through selected texts, seeks to explore two key aspects: first, how Renaissance women were portrayed by the male writing class, and second, how some women of the period actively and vocally engaged in writing and publishing to re-fashion, interpret, and comment on the world around them. The course offers an innovative, interdisciplinary analysis of Renaissance women writers, while also providing an overview of current feminist approaches. It argues for the critical importance of reconsidering Renaissance writers in today’s context, inviting reflection on what these historical voices have to offer now and, in the future, and how our past continues to inform the present, and vice versa.

Focusing on literature by and about women in the Renaissance, the course is structured into biweekly modules, each featuring a single author and their primary text(s). These readings are supported by two scholarly articles per module, each offering unique perspectives on the text and its themes. By synthesizing these articles in their analysis of the primary readings, students engage with critical scholarship, practice analytical skills, and participate in the broader scholarly conversation surrounding both Early Modern Women’s literature and contemporary feminist theory.

ENL3231.title: Restoration Literature
description: This course is a historical survey of British Literature during the Restoration Era (1660-1700). In this course you will be introduced to major Restoration thinkers, including John Milton, the Earl of Rochester and Aphra Behn. You will be tasked to think historically about Restoration literature in order to generate focused and convincing analytical arguments based on close reading of literary and non-literary texts (i.e. recognizing, understanding, and explaining a text's formal and content-based elements).

ENL3296.title: Gothic Literature
description: A study of Gothic literature (prose, poetry, drama) in the British Isles and its cultural contexts. We will map out the trajectory of black presence in British Literature using the lenses of history, politics, and culture. We will observe Britain’s painful process of naming/ renaming of the black presence, and the blackness’s literary and political struggle to make its existence noted in the imagined literary community of British Literature. Reading materials of this class will cover 20th century British literature.

ENL3451.title: Topics in British Literature
description: "Tolkien’s Bookshelf".

As Gandalf, Aragorn, Gimli, and Legolas approach Théoden’s hall in Rohan, Aragon begins to chant in a language unknown to the elf and dwarf and, as Legolas guesses it to be the language of the Rohirrim, the future king offers a translation: “Where now the horse and the rider? Where is the horn that was blowing? / Where is the helm and the hauberk, and the bright hair flowing? / Where is the hand on the harpstring, and the red fire glowing? / Where is the spring and the harvest and the tall corn growing?” As any good bit of worldbuilding, this poetic digression gives the audience some sense of the people of Rohan and their culture. It also tells us a bit about Tolkien the author. Tolkien’s day job was as a professor of medieval English literature at Oxford, and one of the early medieval poems he undoubtedly studied was one now called The Wanderer, which has a familiar ring to its middle section: “What has become of the horse? What has become of the warrior? What has become of the treasure-giver? / What has become of the banquet-seats? Where are the hall-revelries?” As is evident in this example, Tolkien developed a deep knowledge of early English and other literatures produced by the cultures of northwestern Europe, which influenced his work as a fantasy author. In this course, we will read translations of the works (mostly medieval) that inspired Tolkien: Old English poems, Norse mythology and poetry, and Finnish epic, among others. Though the focus of this class will largely be on the works that inspired Tolkien rather than his work, we will read some of his poetry, shorter fiction, as well as sections from The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

ENL4273.title: Modern British Literature
description: "Note: Although this is a 4000-level literature course, the ENG 3014 prerequisite has been waived. To enroll in this course students must have completed ENC 1102 with a C or better.” If you think it’s redundant, just leave out.)
POST-1865.

In her 1919 essay “Modern Fiction” Virginia Woolf complained that real life could not be captured by conventional fiction: “if a writer were a free man … if he could write what he chose, not what he must, if he could base his work upon his own feeling and not upon convention, there would be no plot, no comedy, no tragedy, no love interest or catastrophe in the accepted style.” This course will examine the impetus in Modernism to generate new aesthetic modes, beyond “the accepted style” of previous generations, in order to represent the often-cataclysmic social changes in the first half of the twentieth century. We will explore how works of literature challenge conventional expectations as they experiment with form and content and as they grapple with problems of changing gender roles, of the devastation of WWI, and of the legacies of colonialism and racism at the end of the British Empire. This course is a W course, which means that it is entirely online. Students must have reliable access to a computer and Internet. Students will be expected to complete all reading assignments, to participate regularly and productively in online individual and group assignments, to conduct independent research, and to write literary analyses.

ENL4303.title: British Authors
description: PRE-1865 (or MAJOR AUTHOR) and DIVERSITY. The British author we will focus on in this class is Jane Austen. We will read all 6 of her published novels: Northanger Abbey, Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park, Emma and Persuasion, and a short biography of Austen.
We will read a novel and one or two articles every two weeks. There will be weekly discussions, weekly quizzes, a 10-page research essay and a final exam.

ENL4333.title: Shakespeare Studies
description: PRE-1865 or MAJOR AUTHOR.

In this course, students will read plays from Shakespeare's tenure as chief dramatist for The Lord Chamberlain's Men and, later, The King's Men. Our discussions will involve close analysis of Shakespeare’s language, cultural context, and the various moral, political, and aesthetic issues raised in his plays and poetry.

Rather than following a strict chronological order, we will take a thematic approach, allowing for a deeper exploration of key motifs such as kingship and kinship, gender, love, friendship, and reciprocal obligation. We will also examine domestic and political tyranny, revenge, and moral redemption. The course will incorporate interdisciplinary perspectives, connecting Shakespeare’s works to Renaissance-era visual art and cinema. Additionally, we will engage with contemporary critical theories to explore Shakespeare’s enduring relevance in today’s world. Plays will be supplemented by readings in Shakespearean criticism and contemporary theory. The course is structured into weekly modules, each dedicated to a single author and primary text(s). These primary readings will be supported by two scholarly articles per module, each offering unique perspectives. Through synthesis and analysis of these sources, students will engage with critical scholarship and contribute to broader discussions in Early Modern literature and contemporary theory. By undertaking close readings of Shakespeare’s texts, alongside visual artifacts such as Renaissance paintings, this course will provide insight into Early Modern culture and explore broader themes of cultural identity, nationhood, and individuality.

ENL4341.title: Milton and His Age
description: PRE-1865 (or MAJOR AUTHOR).

Who’s afraid of John Milton? In posing this question, the course aims to analyze Milton’s powerful and decisive influence and impact on the English literary Canon. This course focuses on John Milton’s lyric and epic poetry, prose, and letters, with a particular emphasis on his biblical epic, Paradise Lost.
Published in 1667, Milton’s poem tells the story of Adam and Eve’s disobedience, their exile from Eden, and Satan’s war against God himself.

Written in the aftermath of the English Civil War, Paradise Lost is an epic that explores the themes of free will, gender, obedience and defiance, republicanism, and the nature of good and evil. The seminar aims to facilitate a close reading of Milton’s poem and its themes, while introducing seminal critical interpretations and current critical/theoretical debates.

Undertaking close readings of specific Milton’s texts as well as visual artefacts such as engravings and paintings, the course provides a unique insight into Milton and Early Modern’s culture and helps refashion, re-map broader issues that engage the then emergent status of cultural and religious identity, nation, and individuality. Finally, the course argues for the critical importance of thinking Milton now. We will therefore consider what Milton has to offer now (in an age of global cultures) and in the future.

LIN3010.title: Principles of Linguistics
description: Do you use "friend" as a verb? Why do some people say "aks" and not "ask"? How many different ways can you use the word like? When does “I’m busy” mean “no”? In this course, we will study the English language and how it works. We will connect technical linguistic information to your daily experiences with language. We will learn and practice techniques for describing English, both its words and sentences and larger elements of discourse in context. In linguistic terms, we’ll cover phonology, morphology, semantics, pragmatics, speech act theory, and language variation.

LIN4105.title: History of English Language
description: Beowulf, the oldest narrative poem in the English language, begins: Hwæt! We Gar-Dena in geardagum þeodcyninga þrym gefrunon, hu þa æþelingas ellen fremedon.
There’s not much here that looks anything close to the language we speak today.

How can this be called English!? But, upon closer inspection, there are certain recognizable words: weremains unchanged in Modern English as a plural pronoun; hwæt, though it uses a strange letter in the middle, becomes “what,” as spelling conventions switched around the “h” and “w”; the “g” in gear was pronounced with a “y”-sound, and when spelling caught up with pronunciation, became “year.” Though these lines look like a completely different language, there are hints of the English we speak today even within this excerpt. How did the English of Beowulf become the language that we use daily? How did its sounds, spellings, syntax, and vocabulary change so drastically over time? These are the key questions of this course, which introduces students to basic linguistic concepts while we explore the constantly changing English language from its earliest forms, stretching back around fourteen hundred years ago, to its variations and dialects spoken in the present. As we journey through this long history together, we’ll consider topics such as: why does Old English look like a foreign language? What are English’s closest linguistic relatives? How did contact with other languages and cultures shape English throughout its history? Is English more difficult than other languages? Why do people always complain about English spelling?
Where does the idea of “proper” English come from?

LIN4660.title: Linguistics and Literature
description: This semester, we'll work on two prestigious lexicography projects: We will antedate words for the Oxford English Dictionary. Then, we will work on the NEH-funded Noah Webster's Dictionary Online project. You will learn everything you need to know to join the interdisciplinary team that is getting the project ready for its first-stage launch on April 14, 2028. Topics include: archival research, proofreading, XML markup, image editing, beta testing.

The course emphasizes learning by doing the work. This course is a Research-Intensive (RI) course that involves active engagement in a guided line of inquiry through a process of research or academic scholarship; you will actively learn about digital archive research in this course. Please contact Dr. Beth Young for more information (byoung@ucf.edu).

LIN4680.title: Modern English Grammar
description: To study Grammar from the perspective of Linguistics is to focus on how English is actually spoken, so as to prepare students for working in editorial, writing, and publishing jobs in the professional world. Focusing on the ten types of sentences, the Linguistics approach permits us to study language not only from its logical framework, but to search the COCA for an accurate map of how English is used in print today and how what is grammatically acceptable is evolving to match those trends.
Assignments include weekly quizzes, COCA-searching assignments, test, final exam, Yellowdig discussions.

LIN5137.title: Linguistics
description: PR:

Graduate status or senior standing or C.I. Modern linguistic theories and studies focusing on language acquisition and development, contemporary American English, semantics, and para-linguistics. Occasional.
Do you use friend as a verb? Why do some people say aks and not ask?

How many different ways can you use the word like? When does I’m busy mean no? In this course, we will connect technical linguistic information to your daily experiences with language. We will learn and practice techniques for describing English, from its sounds and words and sentences and larger elements of discourse in context. We will develop an intimate working knowledge of several dictionaries, including the OED. We will investigate linguistic issues empirically with research corpora. In linguistic terms, we’ll cover phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and lexicography.

Because this class is offered as a W class, we will never meet f2f. Your work will be completed on Webcourses (accessed through my.ucf.edu and then the "Online Course Tools" tab). Please check Webcourses daily to be sure you don’t miss anything. You will need reliable access to a computer with internet access. In a pinch, there are computers accessible to you in all UCF's computer labs.

LIT2110.title: World Literature Ⅰ
description: THIS IS A GEP CLASS THAT WILL NOT APPLY TOWARD THE MAJOR OR MINOR AS A LITERARY HISTORY CLASS.

Trickster figures will be the focus of this survey of early world literature. We will examine this complex character at various times, spaces, and places, from the Greeks to the Mayans to Shakespeare. We will investigate how these figures work within and beyond their varied cultural contexts. Sometimes, our discussion will focus on individual characters, sometimes it may focus on authors, and sometimes the trickster element will be more implicit than explicit.

LIT2120.title: World Literature Ⅱ
description: THIS IS A GEP CLASS THAT WILL NOT APPLY TOWARD THE MAJOR OR MINOR AS A LITERARY HISTORY CLASS.

This course introduces the student to writers from around the world whose works span the period from the 1600s to the 2000s. Selections include poetry, prose, and drama and includes the study of voices that have been neglected in the traditional literary canon.

LIT3192.title: Caribbean Literature
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This on-line course traces how Caribbean societies have achieved self-expression through a variety of cultural forms, including documentary writing (history, slave narrative, diplomatic correspondence), literary prose and poetry, and popular culture (dub poetry, music).

LIT3212.title: Research & Writing About Lit
description: LIT 3212 is designated as a Research-Intensive (RI) course. This designation will be noted on your transcripts. Your active engagement in the research and/or creative scholarship process will be the core of your learning experience in this course. A significant portion of your grade for LIT 3212 will be derived from both your active participation in the research process and the tangible course-related project(s) that comes out of said project. If you have any questions about this designation, please ask your course instructor.

Detailed Description: This course walks you through the process of conducting literary research while helping to refine your library skills. Along the way, we will draw from the Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) Information Literacy Framework.

According to the ACRL, “Research is iterative and depends upon asking increasingly complex or new questions whose answers lead to additional questions or lines of inquiry in any field.” We will discuss this concept more in-depth throughout the course. Your goal in the course is to produce a research paper suitable for publication in a literary studies journal.
The course will also focus on a research project created by Jada, an English major who conducted a literary study of James Baldwin’s classic short story, “Sonny’s Blues.”

The basic textbook we will be using for our class is Strategies for Conducting Literary Research, 2e, an Open Educational Resource (meaning it’s free!). It has loads of concepts and vocabulary, some of which you may not have encountered before. In a research-based course, your instructor may require you to write a research paper of 6-12 pages, but the knowledge you need to perform this task can fill up dozens or hundreds of pages. Writing about literature is a complicated, often messy process; it needs to meet high standards while incorporating knowledge from other fields such as psychology, history, science, and other arts. It entails knowledge about language, genre, structures, styles, and more. To produce good research about literature, we need to know a lot of things about a lot of things!

LIT3313H.title: Honors Science Fiction Lit
description: POST-1865. ONLY OPEN TO HONORS STUDENTS.

This class offers a historical overview of the genre of SF from the end of the nineteenth century to the contemporary period. We will cover the birth of the genre in the 1890s, the pulp magazine era, the Golden Age of the 40s-50s, the New Wave revolution of the 60-70s, the Cyberpunk movement of the 80s, and end with a smattering of some of the various styles that characterize SF in the past few decades including Afrofuturism, New British Space Opera, and literary sf. Our overall concern throughout the class will be twofold: first, to stress that SF is a genre with a history and that most individual works of SF can only be adequately interpreted in response to that history, and second, to work against the tendency to see science fiction as an essentially escapist genre by striving to connect our novels and stories to their historical, cultural, and political contexts.

LIT3383.title: Women in Literature
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This upper-level literature elective covers six novels by six contemporary women in six weeks. Focus is on women and girls facing environmental and social justice challenges as they navigate the process of coming of age. Writers studied: Hegland, Alvarez, Ozeki, Hogan, Morrison, and one graphic novelist. Weekly essay postings, discussions, and quizzes. Final exam.

LIT3393.title: Lit & Culture of Trauma
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

According to the National Council for Behavioral Health, “70% of adults in the U.S. have experienced some type of traumatic event at least once in their lives.” While a stubborn stigma remains attached to the public debate on mental health, such a debate has nonetheless increasingly recognized that trauma has become a common feature of contemporary life, leading some observers to claim that we live in an “age of trauma.” Indeed, everyday depictions of trauma populate the cultural landscape, afflicting such fictionalized characters as Katniss Everdeen in The Hunger Games sequels, Tony Stark in Iron Man 3, and Wanda Maximoff of Marvel’s Disney+ series, WandaVision. This new undergraduate course in the Department of English will join the burgeoning field of what’s become known as trauma studies in the humanities by taking up the representation of trauma in a wide range of literary and cultural texts. Although we will draw on scholarship conversant with the medical humanities, for the most part our attention will be given to the ways by which trauma, variously conceived and rendered in narrative form, appears in literary works (novels, short stories, and poems), along with a few films (fiction, documentary, and animated).

LIT3437.title: Global Lit of Enviro Justice
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.

This course focuses on literary and creative works from different genres and international authors addressing issues and stories related to environmental justice themes, such as toxics and land use. This semester, we will examine literary representations of environmental justice from interdisciplinary and cross-cultural perspectives. Instead of focusing on post-apocalyptic fiction, we will read texts that portray environmental change as mundane. We will trace the patterns, and possible solutions, that emerge when we apply environmental humanities methods to complex ecological issues like sustainability, environmental justice, climate change, energy, and water, and begin thinking ecologically about vital planetary interconnections. Ultimately, through critical and creative modes of enquiry, we will strive to understand how artistic and creative expression might enable us to imagine more equitable futures. We will look at a variety of media and genres, which writers and artists have utilized to criticize the present and imagine alternative futures: fiction, poetry, environmental essays and film.

LIT3482.title: Literature & Popular Culture
description: POST-1865.
Zombies: Undead Media from the Gothic to the Algorithm.

This course investigates the zombie narrative in popular culture, exploring its prevalence in global literature, archives, cinema, and interactive media. Tracing the undead from Haitian Vodou narratives and gothic fiction to contemporary graphic novels and post-apocalyptic algorithms, the course asks how speculative texts invoke the folkloric figure of the zombie to express very real socio-cultural anxieties about systemic failure and public health. Students will examine how authors throughout the centuries have drawn upon contemporaneous scientific discourse and tropes of contagion, containment, and human panic to express these fears. Students engage in archival detective work by exploring Zora Neale Hurston’s Tell My Horse alongside 1980s reporting on the Clairvius Narcisse case in medical journals like The Lancet, and are invited to evaluate narrative 'zombie architecture' across nineteenth-century travelogues, East Asian novels, and video games. The course provides opportunities for students to communicate their research through traditional written modes (critical research essays), interdisciplinary methods (field interviews), and technologically innovative, public-facing formats (podcasts and digital storytelling projects).

LIT3482H.title: Honors Literature & Popculture
description: Post-1865.
Only open to Honors students.
A analysis of media to determine popular values in the formation of popular cultural perceptions.

This course focuses on literature, film, photography, online media, museums, and artistic productions related to the contemporary global ecological crisis. We will analyze literary and visual materials on climate change, pollution, and toxic environments, and environmental activism, among other topics. We will explore a range of cultural theory that introduces students to debates on the Anthropocene, species extinction, post-human natures, and planetary futures.

LIT3605.title: Literature and War
description: POST-1865. This course will explore the complex relation between literature and war in the 20th Century by pursuing a set of questions for which there are no easy answers: To what extent has literature been responsible for mythologizing war and thus reproducing the very desire that makes militarism alluring? Is literature capable of conveying what war is like through a conventional aesthetic of realism or are other literary modes better equipped to represent such brutal reality? Is there a limit to the capacity of literature to document the horrors of war, horrors that are otherwise unspeakable? Is literature tasked by society with an obligation to act as the conscience of a nation, a form of ethical reflection on the causes and consequences of war? While the course will mostly focus on more traditional forms of literature (poetry, fiction, memoir), we will also make use of recent developments in literary theory that have expanded the notion of a “text,” allowing us to include a wider range of cultural forms (graphic novel, documentary and fiction film, online sources).

LIT3607.title: Mad Bad & Dangerous
description: In this “a-typical” literature course, as a class, students are asked to consider the nature of creativity, great literary writers of the 18th century through the 20th centuries, and correlations between “the creative mind” and mental illness. The overarching question asked within the course is, “Where does this thing called "[creative] madness" (or melancholy, mania, moroseness) in association with "genius" creativity come from, and at what cost?”

Students examine the creative minds of historical literary writers through their writings (both private letters and published works), and our core text, Touched With Fire (Dr. Kay Redfield Jamison) to consider the mystique, stereotypes, and artistic temperament in association with creativity and “creative genius." In addition, we will read Byron’s Poetry and Prose (a Norton Critical Edition) during full semesters along with Daniel Quinn’s Ishmael. Summer sections will read Ishmael, and examine selected readings from the Byron text.

Objectives: Through engagement with the required texts, Go to Class assignments, discussions, and academic writing, students are encouraged to produce original thinking in the form of scholarly writing and activities. We explore questions about literary writers in attempt to come to a deeper understanding of the creative mind, mental illness, writing methods, and (perhaps most importantly) to experience these writers not as just “historical figures” but as individual human beings. Students will then consider how 21st century student writers and scholars of literature see themselves as writers/authors in relation to historical depictions of literary writers. This endeavor is accomplished through thought-provoking exercises, assignments, and discussion.

After completing this course, students will have an increased ability and knowledge allowing identification of misrepresentations of authors due to bias, foundational knowledge of mental health in association with well-known writers and poets, gain confidence in forming informed opinions, gain experience in using inter-disciplinary methods as fuel for original thinking, the ability to perform academic research to high standards, critically analyze sources as well as cross reference material for accuracy of information on literary writers, and examine literary works for evidence of "authorial self" or author-bias within the writing. The work of the course includes analytical writing, class content contribution and discussion, and a final paper.

LIT3714.title: Literary Modernism
description: POST-1865.

This class puts modernist literature in context by exploring its relationship to the modernist movement across the arts. It treats the modernist movement in literature and art as a set of practices: aesthetic or formal strategies applied to poetry, novels, manifestoes, paintings, films, music, and essays. It also studies modernism as a period of literary and artistic innovations, addresses cultural questions, and the relationship of the arts to mass media and modern politics.

LIT3931.title: Topics in World Literature
description: "Languages of Romance".

What is “romance?” What we’ve meant by the term shifts uneasily: it can be a genre, a term for the novel, any text in “vernacular,” and – principally now – a love story. Neither the term nor the literature that carries its name have remained constant. “Romance” proves remarkably malleable, travelling across the languages of the Mediterranean and North Seas: from the chivalric to the provocative, from poetry to prose. In this class, we will explore “romance” texts, centering on their medieval origins and preoccupations with courtly love, quests, love triangles, and knightly adventures across language and cultural divides, seeing how they influence and build upon each other.

LIT3932.title: Topics in Popular Fiction
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.
This section of Topics in Popular Fiction is subtitled “Tales from the Other(ed)

Side: Literary Re-visions.” We will read contemporary retellings that are based on a variety of texts, including Greek & Roman epics, fairy & folk tales, myths, legends, and more. It isn’t necessary for you to know all of the “original” texts before you read these retellings although it may be more enjoyable if you do know them. One of our collective goals this semester will be to explore those older texts from different angles and to consider how and why these newer, updated versions might still be relevant.

LIT3933.title: Literature and Law
description: POST-1865.
In this course, we will read texts that think philosophically about acts of violence (Arendt, Benjamin, Zizek) and connect these ideas to issues and ideas of justice.

Through this matrix of violence and justice, we will read literature that includes instances, scenarios, scenes, and characters of vigilante action and discuss the role violence plays in constructing ideas of justice. By using the various and complex categories of violence to understand how it is seemingly permissible in some instance and not in others, we can then begin to understand how language shapes representations of certain actions as a means to claim or legitimize these actions as a form of “justice.” Along with the philosophical, there will be legal ramifications that emphasize or, again, legitimize state and individual actors. We will also attend to the various arguments about the violence of law and laws, as well as the violence of language.

LIT4043.title: Modern Drama As Literature
description: POST-1865.

This class explores modern drama (since the 19th century) from cross-disciplinary and cross-cultural perspectives. Theorists of drama stake claims about the most effective ways for dramatists to effect change in audiences and in the world. Tragic dramas, from the earliest in ancient Greece to the most recent, have confronted foolishness, traumatic loss, and the psychic wounds they produce. Comic dramas create critical distance, enabling thought that can lead to personal and/or collective action. Modern playwrights have experimented with the forms and materials of tragedies and comedies and have created genres such as tragicomedy, which combines elements from tragedy and comedy. Newer forms of drama include ethnographic, avant-garde, and performance art, which push the boundaries of drama.

This course presents works of drama and theory from a diverse group of playwrights and authors. Reading drama is never the same as experiencing a live performance, yet the texts of the drama deserve our attention as literature. This course consists of modules, readings, assignments, discussions, and quizzes aimed at improving our understanding of drama and the impact drama has had on our world.

LIT4244.title: World Authors
description: POST-1865 and DIVERSITY.
Rabindranath Tagore was the world’s first non-European writer to win the Novel Prize in Literature in 1913. He is widely celebrated Asia, indeed noted worldwide.

Tagore was a prolific a poet, novelist, essayist, song writer, playwright, and artist. In this course, we will learn of the crisis in representing and reading Tagore, his visionary thinking in terms of gender, nation, religion, and also study some of his art, short stories and nonfiction. We will watch some adapted films that continue to be made from his short stories and novels and hear some songs by Tagore that have shaped South Asian nation-states. Tagore’s significance as a world author cannot be stressed enough. His writings create an enormous oeuvre of exploring some of the most important themes of colonial and postcolonial India.

LIT4433.title: Literature of Science and Tech
description: In the Literature of Science and Technology, we focus on three main themes - language and technology; the body and technology; and identity and technology - in fiction, creative non-fiction, and technical communication. Assignments include two textual analyses, which you will revise into a final 10-page synthesis paper, as well as one short creative writing assignment and a final course reflection.

LIT6276.title: Teaching College Literature
description: What happens in a college literature course? What are we teaching? (And why are we teaching it?) What do we want students to take away from our literature courses? In this course will seek to answer these questions, with a combination of theoretical, historical, and practical approaches. We will read pedagogical-theoretical examinations of the teaching of literature and historical accounts of literary studies curricula. We will reflect on our own experiences in the classroom and discuss issues such as: teaching difficult or controversial content, balancing course flexibility and rigor, and fostering a productive and engaged intellectual community. At the same time, students will undertake, individually and in groups, the “nuts and bolts” work of developing and revising syllabi, assignments, rubrics, in-class activities, and online course content. Students will also craft teaching philosophy statements and prep responses to teaching questions in job interviews. At the end of the semester, students will compile teaching portfolios that include final versions of their teaching philosophy, syllabi, assignments, and other materials.

LIT6435.title: Rhetoric of Science
description: LIT 6435 will be a general approach to the rhetoric of science–kairos, ethos, pathos, logos, and stasis theory —with specific attention to the discourse and paradigm shifts in science as described by Thomas Kuhn. The general text for the book will be Sharon Crowley and Debra Hawhee's Ancient Rhetorics for Contemporary Students. Additionally, we will be reading four chapters from Elizabeth Kolbert's The Sixth Extinction with some attendant articles from traditional scientific journals such as Nature on genomic studies and the Anthropocene epoch that Kolbert bases her "popular science" or "journalistic science" work on. We will also look at position papers from the Union of Concerned Scientists on global warming and several chapters from David George Haskell's The Forest Unseen.
Haskell is a biologist by training but he employs a lot of figurative language in his writing so we will examine his literary style.

This is both a core course and a restricted elective in the Technical Communication track, but graduate students majoring in Literary, Cultural and Textual Studies; Creative Writing; Writing and Rhetoric; and the Texts and Technology Ph.D. program are also welcome.

LIT6936.title: Studies in Lct Theory
description: This seminar offers an introduction to the interdisciplinary field of fan studies, examining the practices, politics, and pleasures of fan communities across media platforms and cultural contexts. We will explore how fans create meaning, build identity, and form community through transformative works — from fan fiction to cosplay, data-making, and AI-generated content — while attending to the infrastructures, platforms, and archives that shape what fan participation looks like and who gets to participate. The course takes seriously the uneven terrain of fandom: how identity, social location, and nationality structure fan experience and scholarly inquiry alike, reading across both Anglophone and transnational fandoms. We will also grapple with fandom's contentious dimensions, including harassment and reactionary movements increasingly playing out in participatory spaces. Students will leave with fluency in foundational and cutting-edge scholarship, preparation to conduct original fan studies research, and critical tools for thinking about what fandom reveals about media, identity, and digital culture more broadly.
